best-broadway-shows.intro:
# Best Broadway Shows in March 2026

Broadway enters the spring season with a robust lineup that balances innovative new works with beloved classics. This month's top-rated shows span from groundbreaking contemporary musicals to time-tested revivals, offering theatergoers an impressive range of storytelling styles and theatrical experiences.

Leading the pack is **Hamilton**, which continues to prove why it transformed the American musical landscape. Lin-Manuel Miranda's hip-hop retelling of Alexander Hamilton's life maintains its position as a must-see theatrical event, earning the highest critical marks with a 90/100 rating. Close behind, **Maybe Happy Ending** emerges as one of the season's most delightful surprises—a tender robot love story that critics are calling one of Broadway's most original musicals in years.

The comedy front is equally strong, with **Oh, Mary!** delivering absurdist laughs through Cole Escola's irreverent take on Mary Todd Lincoln, while **The Book of Mormon** continues its long run as Broadway's reigning satirical champion. Meanwhile, spectacle remains alive and well through **The Lion King**'s iconic puppetry and **Harry Potter and the Cursed Child**'s stage magic.

This month also brings a timely revival of **Ragtime**, which resonates with contemporary audiences through its examination of race, immigration, and justice in early 20th-century America. Rounding out the top ten are the mythic folk-opera **Hadestown**, the music-driven **Buena Vista Social Club**, and the enduring cynicism of **Chicago**.

With an average critic score of 83/100 across these ten productions, March 2026 represents a particularly strong moment for Broadway quality and diversity. Whether you're drawn to innovative storytelling, spectacular stagecraft, or sharp-witted comedy, this month's lineup offers compelling reasons to experience live theater.

best-broadway-shows-2020.intro:
# Best Broadway Shows from 2020

As we look back from March 2026, the Broadway season of 2020 stands as one of the most truncated in theater history, with the pandemic shuttering theaters that March and leaving only a handful of productions to complete their critical runs. Yet the shows that did open before the shutdown reveal a season marked by bold artistic choices and long-overdue revivals.

**Les Misérables** leads our rankings with its grittier reboot at the newly refurbished Sondheim Theatre, offering audiences a fresh take on the beloved musical that divides purists while winning over those hungry for reinvention. **A Soldier's Play** represents perhaps the season's most significant achievement—Charles Fuller's Pulitzer Prize-winning drama finally receiving its Broadway premiere in a stellar production that proves the work's examination of race and power within the military remains unnervingly relevant decades after it was written.

The season also showcases intimate theatrical experiences, with **My Name is Lucy Barton** presenting Laura Linney in a solo performance that critics find either luminous or limited, depending on their appetite for quiet introspection. Meanwhile, **Grand Horizons** offers more traditional boulevard comedy pleasures elevated by Jane Alexander's expert touch, and Ivo van Hove's **West Side Story** reimagining proves predictably polarizing, with its radical staging choices earning both passionate defenders and harsh detractors.

With an average critical score of 74/100 across these five productions, the abbreviated 2020 season ultimately presents a mixed but intriguing snapshot of Broadway at a crossroads—caught between reverence for classic material and the impulse to radically reimagine it. For theatergoers interested in this pivotal moment, these productions offer essential viewing into what Broadway was becoming before everything changed.

best-broadway-shows-2021.intro:

The highest-rated show from this period is **Dana H.**, an unconventional docudrama that continues to polarize and mesmerize audiences with Deirdre O'Connell's extraordinary lip-sync performance to a real interview recording. Critics describe it as unlike anything else on Broadway, pushing the boundaries of what theatrical performance can be.

Close behind are two very different revivals: **Cabaret at the Kit Kat Club**, which transforms the August Wilson Theatre into an immersive nightclub experience under Rebecca Frecknall's direction, and **The Phantom of the Opera**, which critics acknowledge as campy yet undeniably spectacular, with Andrew Lloyd Webber's infectious melodies proving their staying power.

The season also showcases powerful solo performances in **Lackawanna Blues**, where Ruben Santiago-Hudson embodies dozens of characters, and **Is This a Room**, which transforms a verbatim FBI transcript into gripping theater. Meanwhile, Marianne Elliott's gender-swapped **Company** offers a fresh perspective on Sondheim's classic musical.

With an average critic score of 81/100 across these ten productions, the 2021 season delivered consistently strong work across multiple genres—from Lynn Nottage's workplace drama **Clyde's** to the pop-concert energy of **SIX**. Whether you're drawn to experimental theater or classic Broadway spectacle, these shows offer a snapshot of an industry rebuilding itself with both courage and creativity.

best-broadway-shows-2022.intro:

As of March 2026, the exceptional class of 2022 continues to resonate as one of Broadway's most artistically significant seasons in recent memory. Four years later, these productions remain essential viewing for theater enthusiasts seeking substance alongside spectacle.

Leading the pack is **Kimberly Akimbo**, David Lindsay-Abaire and Jeanine Tesori's quirky musical about a teenager with a rare aging condition. Critics consistently praise its remarkable tonal balance, finding both hilarious comedy and genuine emotional depth in what could have been merely a high-concept premise. The show exemplifies 2022's tendency toward intimate, character-driven storytelling over spectacle.

**Into the Woods** and **A Strange Loop** tie for second place, representing opposite ends of the theatrical spectrum. The Sondheim revival offers a stripped-down interpretation that honors the late composer's legacy with clarity and purpose, while Michael R. Jackson's Pulitzer-winning meta-musical breaks new ground with its brazenly original exploration of a Black queer artist's creative process. Both demonstrate that Broadway in 2022 embraced artistic risk-taking alongside reverent revival work.

The season's remarkable depth extends beyond the top three. Four Pulitzer Prize-winning plays—**Topdog/Underdog**, **Leopoldstadt**, **Between Riverside and Crazy**, and **How I Learned to Drive**—brought literary heft to Broadway stages, while **Cost of Living** and **Ain't No Mo'** tackled disability and race with unflinching honesty. Even solo performer **Mike Birbiglia** earned critical acclaim typically reserved for full-scale productions.

With an average critic score of 83/100 across these ten productions, the 2022 season set a high bar for artistic achievement that subsequent years continue to chase. For those exploring Broadway's current landscape, these shows represent the foundation of contemporary theatrical excellence.

The wide variance in reception—from enthusiastic praise to lukewarm responses—underscores how even well-known properties require fresh creative vision to resonate with contemporary audiences.

As more productions open and accumulate reviews throughout the spring, theatergoers should monitor how these shows develop and which productions gain momentum with both critics and audiences.

best-broadway-plays-2020.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays Opening in 2020

As we look back from March 2026 at the plays that premiered on Broadway in 2020, we're examining a collection shaped by extraordinary circumstances—a season that began with promise before theaters went dark that spring, with several productions managing only brief runs before the pandemic shutdown.

Among the standout productions from this truncated year, **A Soldier's Play** earns the highest marks for its long-overdue Broadway debut. Charles Fuller's Pulitzer Prize-winning drama about racism and violence in a World War II-era army base proves its themes remain urgently relevant, with critics praising the production's powerful performances across 29 reviews. Meanwhile, **Les Misérables** returns in a grittier, reimagined production at the refurbished Sondheim Theatre, earning strong notices for its fresh approach to the classic material, though the radical departure from the beloved original staging doesn't win over all traditionalists.

**My Name is Lucy Barton** showcases Laura Linney in a solo performance adapted from Elizabeth Strout's novel, with critics divided between those captivated by Linney's luminous work and those who find the stage adaptation wanting. Bess Wohl's **Grand Horizons** offers lighter fare—a boulevard comedy about late-life divorce elevated by veterans Jane Alexander and James Cromwell—while Ivo van Hove's controversial **West Side Story** reimagining provokes the sharpest critical divide with its stark, video-enhanced aesthetic.

With an average critic score of 74/100 across these five productions, 2020's brief theatrical moment offered both timely drama and bold reinvention. Browse our detailed reviews to discover which of these productions might still resonate with your theatrical tastes today.

best-broadway-plays-2021.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays of 2021

As we look back from March 2026, the Broadway shows that opened in 2021 represent a remarkable period of theatrical rebirth. Following the industry's lengthy pandemic shutdown, these productions marked not just a reopening, but a creative renaissance that challenged conventions and embraced bold experimentation.

The ten plays featured in this guide average an impressive 81/100 critic score, reflecting the exceptional quality that defined this era. Leading the field is **Dana H.**, Lucas Hnath's unconventional docudrama featuring Deirdre O'Connell's stunning lip-sync performance, which critics hail as mesmerizing and unforgettable. Close behind, Rebecca Frecknall's immersive reimagining of **Cabaret at the Kit Kat Club** earns widespread acclaim for its complete transformation of the August Wilson Theatre into a decadent nightclub experience.

The season demonstrates remarkable range: from **The Lehman Trilogy**'s epic examination of American capitalism to **Pass Over**'s urgent exploration of Black American life, which appropriately served as Broadway's official reopening production. Experimental works like **Is This a Room**, constructed entirely from FBI transcripts, prove that theatrical innovation thrives alongside reimagined classics like Marianne Elliott's gender-swapped **Company**.

What distinguishes these 2021 productions is their willingness to take risks—whether through unconventional staging, verbatim text, solo virtuosity, or radical reinterpretation of established works. Five years later, these shows continue to influence Broadway's creative direction, proving that the return from shutdown wasn't merely a resumption of business as usual, but a fundamental reconsideration of what theater could be.

Explore our complete rankings below to discover which of these groundbreaking productions best suits your theatrical tastes.

best-broadway-plays-2022.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays from 2022

As we look back from March 2026, the 2022 Broadway season stands out as a remarkable year defined by intimate storytelling, theatrical innovation, and the triumphant return of live performance following the pandemic shutdown. With an impressive average critic score of 83/100 across our featured productions, this season delivered an exceptional concentration of award-winning work that continues to resonate with audiences.

The year's standout achievement is **Kimberly Akimbo**, David Lindsay-Abaire and Jeanine Tesori's quirky musical about a teenager with a rare aging condition. Critics consistently praise its rare ability to balance sharp comedy with genuine emotional depth, earning it the highest marks of the season. Close behind, **Into the Woods** offers a stripped-down revival that serves as a fitting tribute to Stephen Sondheim's legacy, while **A Strange Loop** brings Michael R. Jackson's brazenly original, Pulitzer Prize-winning meta-musical to Broadway with uncompromising honesty.

Notably, 2022 marks an extraordinary year for Pulitzer Prize-winning works on Broadway stages. Five of our featured productions—A Strange Loop, Topdog/Underdog, Between Riverside and Crazy, How I Learned to Drive, and Cost of Living—earned theater's most prestigious honor, showcasing the season's commitment to dramatically significant work. From Tom Stoppard's deeply personal Holocaust meditation **Leopoldstadt** to Jordan E. Cooper's audacious satire **Ain't No Mo'**, the season demonstrates remarkable range in subject matter and theatrical approach.

Whether you're discovering these productions for the first time or revisiting familiar favorites, this collection represents some of the most critically acclaimed theater of the decade.

best-broadway-plays-2023.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays of 2023

As of March 2026, the theatrical landscape continues to be enriched by exceptional plays that premiered in 2023, a year that proved remarkably strong for non-musical drama on Broadway. These productions demonstrate the enduring power of straight plays to tackle everything from intimate family dynamics to sweeping historical narratives, with an average critical score of 82/100 reflecting the consistently high quality across the season.

Leading the field is Maria Friedman's revival of **Merrily We Roll Along**, which earns an 85/100 score and stands as proof that Sondheim's notorious 1981 flop has found redemption through emotionally resonant reimagining. Tied at the top is **Stranger Things: The First Shadow**, the West End transfer that transcends its source material with technically stunning theatrical craft that critics describe as breathtaking.

Close behind, **Appropriate** emerges as a searing family drama that critics are calling a modern masterpiece, anchored by Sarah Paulson's performance and blistering ensemble work. The year also brought timely revivals like **Parade**, which resonates with urgent contemporary relevance, and **Purlie Victorious**, Ossie Davis's 1961 satire that proves bracingly relevant more than six decades later.

Solo performances shine in **Just for Us**, while **Stereophonic**—despite the lowest score on this list at 79/100—earns praise as a masterful, immersive three-hour experience. Other notable entries include a full-scale **Sweeney Todd** revival, the Pulitzer-winning **Fat Ham**, and the music-driven **Buena Vista Social Club**.

For theatergoers seeking the best of dramatic storytelling, these 2023 productions remain essential viewing, offering a diverse range of voices, styles, and perspectives that continue to define contemporary American theater.

best-broadway-plays-2024.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays Opening in 2024

As we look back from March 2026, the 2024 Broadway season stands out as a remarkably diverse and critically acclaimed year for new productions. The ten shows featured in this guide maintain an impressive average critic score of 83/100, reflecting a season that delivered both artistic ambition and audience appeal across multiple genres.

Leading the pack is **Stereophonic**, David Adjmi's meticulously crafted drama about a 1970s rock band in the studio, which critics have hailed as a theatrical marvel for its authentic depiction of the creative process. Close behind is **Operation Mincemeat**, the grassroots British sensation that proved inventive ensemble storytelling could triumph on Broadway after its successful West End run. **Maybe Happy Ending** rounds out the top tier with its unexpectedly moving robot love story, praised as one of Broadway's most original musicals in recent memory.

The year's offerings span from Cole Escola's irreverent **Oh, Mary!**—an absurdist take on Mary Todd Lincoln that became a comedic phenomenon—to the emotional weight of **Mary Jane**, Amy Herzog's intimate examination of parental devotion. Classic revivals also made their mark, with Audra McDonald bringing fresh interpretation to Mama Rose in **Gypsy** and a lavish new production of **Oliver!** reminding audiences why Lionel Bart's musical endures.

Dance-forward **Illinoise** and historically minded **Suffs** demonstrated Broadway's continued appetite for experimental forms and socially conscious storytelling, proving that 2024's theatrical landscape embraced both innovation and tradition.

Whether you're discovering these productions for the first time or revisiting old favorites, this guide offers insights into a season that continues to resonate with theatergoers today.

best-broadway-plays-2025.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays Opening in 2025

As March 2026 arrives, Broadway audiences continue to enjoy an exceptionally strong collection of plays that premiered throughout 2025. This curated selection of ten productions—averaging an impressive 84/100 from critics—demonstrates the breadth and vitality of contemporary American theater, from bold new works to thoughtfully reimagined classics.

The season's highest-rated production, **All My Sons**, finds director Ivo van Hove bringing his signature minimalist aesthetic to Arthur Miller's postwar drama, earning widespread acclaim for its emotional intensity and exceptional ensemble work. Close behind, the 20th-anniversary revival of **The 25th Annual Putnam County Spelling Bee** proves that the quirky musical-comedy still resonates, with critics praising its airtight writing and joyous spirit. Meanwhile, **Paddington The Musical** enchants audiences with what reviewers describe as a remarkably lifelike bear puppet that represents a genuine theatrical marvel.

The lineup reflects Broadway's ongoing commitment to diverse voices and urgent contemporary themes. **Liberation**, Bryna Turner's feminist memory play directed by Whitney White, tackles timely issues through ambitious storytelling, while Sanaz Toossi's Pulitzer Prize-winning **English** offers a sensitive exploration of language and identity. The season also features two major musical revivals—**Ragtime**, powered by Joshua Henry's acclaimed performance, and **Dead Outlaw**, David Yazbek's darkly comic rock musical about the bizarre afterlife of outlaw Elmer McCurdy.

Whether you're drawn to intimate character studies, spectacular family entertainment, or socially conscious drama, this season offers something for every theatergoer. Check individual show pages for detailed reviews, ticket information, and current performance schedules.

best-broadway-plays-2026.intro:
# Best Broadway Plays of 2026

March 2026 brings a notably lean opening schedule for new Broadway plays, with just one production making its debut this month. While the limited roster reflects the challenging economics facing straight plays on Broadway, the sole entry demonstrates the enduring appeal of well-crafted psychological drama.

**Bug** stands as the month's singular offering, marking the long-awaited Broadway premiere of Tracy Letts' 1996 psychological thriller. With a solid critic score of 74/100 across 35 reviews, the production earns mostly positive notices for its intense exploration of paranoia and delusion. Originally produced by Chicago's Red Orchid Theatre three decades ago, the play arrives on Broadway with renewed relevance, its themes of conspiracy and fractured reality resonating in contemporary discourse. Critics particularly praise the production's claustrophobic staging and committed performances, though some note the material's deliberately unsettling nature may not appeal to all theatergoers.

The sparse March schedule underscores a broader trend in commercial theater, where plays increasingly struggle to secure Broadway berths amid rising production costs and risk-averse producers. That **Bug** makes it to the Great White Way at all speaks to both the strength of Letts' reputation—bolstered by his Pulitzer Prize-winning **August: Osage County**—and the theater community's ongoing commitment to provocative, challenging work.

For audiences seeking substantive dramatic fare this month, **Bug** offers a compelling if confronting option that showcases the raw power of theatrical storytelling. Those planning their spring theater calendar should consider catching this production while monitoring announcements for upcoming play openings in the months ahead.
